title: The Lighthouse · 3
paragraphs: So they’re gone, she thought, sighing with relief and disappointment. Her sympathy seemed to fly back into her face, like a bramble springing back. She felt strangely divided, as if one part of her were drawn out there—it was a still, hazy day; this morning the Lighthouse looked immensely far away—while the other part had planted itself stubbornly, solidly, here on the lawn. She saw her canvas as if it had floated up and set itself, white and uncompromising, right in front of her. With its cold stare it seemed to scold her for all this hurry and agitation, this foolishness and waste of emotion. It called her back sharply, and it spread through her mind first a peace, as her disorderly feelings (he had gone, and she had been so sorry for him, and she had said nothing) marched off the field; and then emptiness. She looked blankly at the canvas, with its uncompromising white stare; from the canvas to the garden. There was something (she stood screwing up her little Chinese eyes in her small puckered face), something she remembered in the way those lines related, cutting across, slicing down, and in the mass of the hedge with its green cave of blues and browns, which had stayed in her mind. It had tied a knot in her mind, so that at odd moments, without meaning to, as she walked along the Brompton Road in London, as she brushed her hair, she found herself painting that picture, running her eye over it, and untying the knot in her imagination. But there was all the difference in the world between this airy planning away from the canvas and actually taking up her brush and making the first mark.

In her agitation at Mr. Ramsay’s being there, she had taken the wrong brush, and her easel, jammed into the ground so nervously, was at the wrong angle. And now that she had put that right, and in doing so had quieted the intrusions and irrelevances that tugged at her attention and reminded her that she was such-and-such a person, with such-and-such relations to people, she took her hand and raised her brush. For a moment it hung trembling in the air in a painful but exciting ecstasy. Where to begin?—that was the question; at what point should she make the first mark? One line placed on the canvas committed her to countless risks, to frequent decisions that could not be undone. Everything that seemed simple in the idea became complicated the moment she put it into practice—just as waves, seen from the top of a cliff, form themselves into symmetrical patterns, but to the swimmer among them are split by steep gulfs and foaming crests. Still, the risk had to be taken; the mark had to be made.

With a strange physical sensation, as if she were being pushed forward and at the same time had to hold herself back, she made her first quick, decisive stroke. The brush came down. It flickered brown over the white canvas; it left a running mark. She did it a second time—a third time. And so, pausing and flickering, she found a dancing, rhythmic movement, as if the pauses were one part of the rhythm and the strokes another, and all were connected. And so, lightly and swiftly pausing, striking, she scored her canvas with brown, running, nervous lines, which had no sooner settled there than they enclosed (she felt it looming out at her) a space. Down in the hollow of one wave she saw the next wave towering higher and higher above her. For what could be more formidable than that space? Here she was again, she thought, stepping back to look at it, drawn out of gossip, out of living, out of fellowship with people, into the presence of this formidable, ancient enemy of hers—this other thing, this truth, this reality, which suddenly seized her, rose up stark behind the appearance of things and demanded her attention. She was half unwilling, half reluctant. Why must she always be drawn out and dragged away? Why not be left in peace, to talk to Mr. Carmichael on the lawn? It was a demanding kind of relationship, anyway. Other objects of worship were content with worship; men, women, God, all let you kneel down flat before them. But this form, even if it was only the shape of a white lampshade looming on a wicker table, roused you to endless combat, challenged you to a fight you were bound to lose. Always (it was in her nature, or in her sex, she did not know which), before she traded the fluidity of life for the concentration of painting, she had a few moments of nakedness, when she seemed like an unborn soul, a soul torn from its body, hesitating on some windy pinnacle and exposed without protection to every blast of doubt. Why, then, did she do it? She looked at the canvas, lightly scored with running lines. It would be hung in the servants’ bedrooms. It would be rolled up and stuffed under a sofa. What was the good of doing it, then? And she heard some voice saying she couldn’t paint, saying she couldn’t create, as if she were caught up in one of those habitual currents which, after a while, form experience in the mind, so that you repeat words without being aware any longer of who first said them.

Can’t paint, can’t write, she murmured in a monotone, anxiously trying to decide on her plan of attack. For the mass loomed up before her; it stuck out; she could feel it pressing on her eyeballs. Then, as if some juice her faculties needed for oiling had squirted out all by itself, she began dipping, uncertainly, among the blues and umbers, moving her brush this way and that. But the brush was heavier now and slower, as though it had fallen in with some rhythm that what she saw was dictating to her (her eyes kept going from the hedge to the canvas), so that while her hand trembled with life, the rhythm was strong enough to carry her along on its current. She was certainly losing her awareness of things outside her. And as she lost awareness of outer things—of her name, her personality, her appearance, of whether Mr. Carmichael was there or not—her mind kept throwing up from its depths scenes and names and sayings and memories and ideas, like a fountain spurting over that glaring, horribly difficult white space, while she shaped it with greens and blues.

That was what Charles Tansley used to say, she remembered: women can’t paint, can’t write. He had come up behind her once and stood right beside her—she hated that—while she was painting here, on this very spot. “Shag tobacco,” he said, “fivepence an ounce,” making a show of his poverty and his principles. (But the war had taken the sting out of her sense of being a woman. Poor devils, you thought, poor devils of both sexes, getting into such messes.) He always had a book tucked under his arm—a purple one. He “worked.” She remembered him sitting at work in a blaze of sunshine. At dinner he would plant himself right in the middle of the view. And then, she reflected, there had been that scene on the beach. That had to be remembered. It was a windy morning, and they had all gone down to the beach. Mrs. Ramsay sat by a rock writing letters. On and on she wrote. At last she looked up at something floating in the sea. “Oh,” she said, “is it a lobster pot? Is it a boat turned upside down?” She was too nearsighted to see it, and at that Charles Tansley became as nice as he possibly could. He started playing ducks and drakes, skipping stones. The two of them picked out small flat black stones and sent them bouncing across the waves. From time to time Mrs. Ramsay looked up over her glasses and laughed at them. What they talked about, she could not remember—only herself and Charles throwing stones, suddenly getting along very well, and Mrs. Ramsay watching. She had been very aware of that. Mrs. Ramsay, she thought, stepping back and narrowing her eyes. (It must have made a big difference to the design when Mrs. Ramsay was sitting on the step with James. There must have been a shadow.) Mrs. Ramsay. Whenever she thought of Charles and herself skipping stones, and of that whole scene on the beach, it all seemed somehow to rest on Mrs. Ramsay sitting under the rock with a pad on her knee, writing letters. (She wrote endless letters, and now and then the wind snatched one, and she and Charles just managed to save a page from the sea.) What power there was in the human soul! she thought. That woman, sitting there writing under the rock, turned everything simple; made these angers and irritations fall away like old rags. She put this together with that, and then with this, and so, out of that wretched silliness and spite (she and Charles, squabbling and sparring, had been silly and spiteful), she made something—this scene on the beach, say, this moment of friendship and liking—that had lasted all these years, whole and complete, so that Lily dipped into it to remake her memory of him, and it stayed in the mind almost like a work of art.

“Like a work of art,” she repeated, looking from her canvas to the drawing-room steps and back again. She had to rest for a moment. And as she rested, looking vaguely from one to the other, the old question that was forever crossing the sky of the soul—the vast, general question which tended to take on a particular shape at moments like these, when she let go of faculties that had been under strain—stood over her, paused over her, darkened over her. What is the meaning of life? That was all—a simple question; one that tended to close in on you as the years went by. The great revelation had never come. Perhaps the great revelation never did come. Instead there were little daily miracles, illuminations, matches struck unexpectedly in the dark; here was one. This, that, and the other; herself and Charles Tansley and the breaking wave; Mrs. Ramsay bringing them together; Mrs. Ramsay saying “Life stand still here”; Mrs. Ramsay making something permanent out of the moment (just as Lily herself, in another sphere, tried to make something permanent out of the moment)—this had the nature of a revelation. In the midst of chaos there was shape; this eternal passing and flowing (she looked at the clouds going by and the leaves shaking) was struck into something stable. Life stand still here, Mrs. Ramsay said. “Mrs. Ramsay! Mrs. Ramsay!” she repeated. She owed this revelation to her.

Everything was silent. Nobody seemed to be stirring in the house yet. She looked at it, sleeping there in the early sunlight, its windows green and blue with the reflected leaves. The faint thought she was having about Mrs. Ramsay seemed in harmony with this quiet house, this smoke, this fine early-morning air. Faint and unreal, it was amazingly pure and exciting. She hoped nobody would open a window or come out of the house, but that she would be left alone to go on thinking, to go on painting. She turned to her canvas. But pushed by some curiosity, driven by the discomfort of the sympathy she was still holding in, unreleased, she walked a step or two to the end of the lawn to see whether, down there on the beach, she could see that little company setting sail. Down there among the little boats floating on the water, some with their sails furled, some moving slowly away, for it was very calm, there was one a little apart from the others. Its sail was being hoisted at that very moment. She decided that there, in that very distant and entirely silent little boat, Mr. Ramsay was sitting with Cam and James. Now they had got the sail up; now, after a little flagging and hesitation, the sails filled, and, wrapped in deep silence, she watched the boat make its way deliberately past the other boats and out to sea.
